Over the preceding 3 months, he had left buttock and greater trochanteric pain, initially attributed to overuse. He denied fevers or systemic symptoms. [Clinical segment 1] A 15-year-old girl presented with multiple swellings of five months’ duration. She noted progressive enlargement of bilateral neck masses and one each on her back and anterior abdominal wall, without pain. There was no significant past medical, personal, or family history.

[Clinical segment 2] On examination, there were seven subcutaneous, nontender, mobile swellings measuring 1×1 to 3×3 cm in the cervical regions, right paraspinal area, and anterior abdominal wall. The lesions were firm to hard without changes in the overlying skin.

[Clinical segment 3] Ultrasonography confirmed that all lesions were confined to the subcutaneous tissue, with no lymphadenopathy or deeper masses.

[Clinical segment 4] Cytology smears from all sites showed moderate cellularity with similar features: predominantly plump spindle cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm, fragments of collagenous matrix, and occasional small cells with scant cytoplasm. The spindle cells had bipolar cytoplasmic extensions and round-to-oval nuclei with fine granular chromatin; nucleoli were inconspicuous. Nuclear hyperchromasia, pleomorphism, or atypicality was not seen, and mitoses were sparse. There was no necrosis or inflammatory cells.

[Clinical segment 5] Complete blood count, metabolic panel, and skeletal survey were all normal. With a clinical impression of lymphoreticular malignancy or metastatic disease, fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) was performed on the most prominent swellings (two cervical, one paraspinal, one abdominal).

[Clinical segment 1] On examination, blood pressure was 113/70 mmHg, pulse 98 beats/min, and temperature 37.5 °C. Abdominal, cardiorespiratory, neurological, and pelvic examinations were unremarkable. Transvaginal ultrasound showed a 13 mm gestational sac with irregular margins and a yolk sac in the anterior isthmic portion of the uterus, raising suspicion for a cesarean-section scar ectopic pregnancy. Doppler was declined. Serial β-hCG measurements rose by 33% over 48 hours (21,521 mIU/mL). The patient missed follow-up and returned 1 week later with 5 days of worsening pelvic pain.

[Clinical segment 2] Repeat transvaginal scan revealed a fetal pole with cardiac activity (crown–rump length 0.9 cm) in a sac traversing the full width of the anterior myometrium, extending exophytically toward the serosa, with trophoblastic flow on Doppler; there was no endometrial fluid or free pelvic fluid. She was taken to laparoscopy and hysteroscopy: the bladder was densely adherent to the anterior uterine wall, the ectopic was not visualized, and extensive intrauterine adhesions obscured the view; there was no intracavitary bleeding. Postoperatively, she became hypotensive (systolic 82–95 mmHg) without vaginal bleeding. This prompted an urgent MRI to map the location of the pregnancy.

[Clinical segment 3] A 36-year-old G5P2+2 woman with two prior cesarean deliveries and two first-trimester miscarriages was referred at 6 weeks of amenorrhea for evaluation of a pregnancy of unknown location. Her serum quantitative β-hCG was 16,124 mIU/mL. A transabdominal ultrasound at presentation did not locate an intrauterine or extrauterine pregnancy. A copper intrauterine device had been removed 2 months before her last menstrual period. She had used one cycle of clomiphene. She had no chronic illnesses, did not smoke or drink, and was not on medications.

[Clinical segment 1] A 32-year-old primigravida at 36 weeks 3 days of gestation presented with acute left lower abdominal pain and vomiting. She denied vaginal bleeding, urinary symptoms, constipation, or changes in bowel habits. Her observations were stable, and she appeared clinically well. On examination, there was slight tenderness in the left abdomen without guarding; the uterus was soft and relaxed. Foetal movements and monitoring were normal.

[Clinical segment 2] At 37 weeks 1 day, her pain worsened with vomiting, and abdominal exam revealed generalized tenderness with guarding in the left iliac fossa. Given the acute abdomen, rising inflammatory markers, and concern for ovarian torsion, the decision was made to proceed with a caesarean section followed by surgical management of the adnexa.

[Clinical segment 3] On admission, Hb was 121 g/L, WCC 10.0 × 10^9/L, neutrophils 9.1 × 10^9/L, platelets 270 × 10^9/L, and CRP 30 mg/L. Over three days, CRP rose to 209 mg/L while WCC remained stable. Repeated transabdominal and transvaginal ultrasounds by an experienced sonographer showed the left adnexal cyst unchanged in size and appearance with no whirlpool sign, stromal oedema, absent Doppler flow, or free pelvic fluid. MRI was considered but not performed due to the rapid clinical change.

[Clinical segment 4] Her antenatal course had been uneventful except for a 70 × 60 × 60 mm left ovarian cyst first noted at 5 weeks and thought to be endometriotic. Follow-up scans at 32 weeks showed the cyst measured 63 × 33 × 69 mm with internal echoes and an avascular solid component. Tumour markers (CEA, CA-19-9, CA-125) were within normal limits, and an MDT review deemed the cyst benign and recommended surveillance.

input_text:
[Clinical segment 1] A 25-year-old man with a history of Hodgkin lymphoma presented with a 2-month history of a gradually enlarging mass over the dorsum of his left hand. Six years earlier, he had been diagnosed with Hodgkin lymphoma on the basis of mediastinal lymphadenopathy and systemic symptoms, and he received 13 courses of chemotherapy. Physical examination at this visit revealed a soft-tissue mass over the second metacarpal dorsum, approximately 4 cm in greatest dimension, with mild tenderness and no limitation of movement. The patient underwent surgical excision of the lesion, and two specimens were submitted to pathology. The larger specimen consisted of gray, gelatinous tissue measuring 4 × 2.5 × 0.8 cm and 0.5 × 0.5 × 0.5 cm. [Clinical segment 1] A 34-year-old Filipino man presented with a 4-month history of left eye proptosis, diplopia, and chemosis without epistaxis, headache, or nasal obstruction. Endoscopic nasal examination revealed a mass at the level of the left middle turbinate extending into the left nasal roof and eroding the upper nasal septum. Ophthalmologic evaluation showed mild left proptosis with full extraocular movements, no papilledema, and normal visual acuity. Contrast-enhanced CT of the paranasal sinuses demonstrated an expansile, mildly enhancing soft-tissue mass in the anterosuperior nasal cavity encroaching on the left orbital cavity, with remodeling of the left medial orbital wall and extension to the level of the cribriform plate, along with retention of secretions in the left frontal sinus. MRI (T1-weighted postcontrast) showed an enhancing mass reaching the nasal vault without dural enhancement or intracranial extension; T2 and non–contrast T1 sequences revealed no intratumoral hemorrhage or cystic change. The patient underwent endoscopic endonasal resection, which disclosed a cystic mass occupying the left fronto-ethmoid region with destruction of the anterior skull base and erosion of the left lamina papyracea; the dura was exposed but intact, and no cerebrospinal fluid leak was noted. A routine functional endoscopic sinus surgery was completed after tumor excision.

[Clinical segment 1] A 5-month-old dark-skinned boy was seen for evaluation of a congenital skin lesion on the left supraclavicular area. At birth, the lesion measured 11 cm × 3.5 cm; at 5 months it measured 10 cm × 2.5 cm. A working diagnosis of probable RICH was made.

[Clinical segment 1] Laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin of 6.5 g/dL and hematocrit of 28%, down from a baseline hemoglobin of 10.5 g/dL and hematocrit of 38% one month prior. A broad differential diagnosis was considered, including urinary calculus, acute pyelonephritis, renal infarction, and musculoskeletal pain; concern was also raised for possible abdominal aortic aneurysm rupture given his vascular risk factors. Point-of-care ultrasound demonstrated heterogeneous echogenicity around the right renal parenchyma. An emergent contrast-enhanced CT scan revealed a large retroperitoneal hemorrhage surrounding the right kidney extending into the pelvis, but the bleeding source could not be identified. The patient was managed conservatively with blood transfusions, but over the next two days he developed worsening anemia and features of hemorrhagic shock. A repeat CT scan showed an expanding hematoma within and outside the renal capsule, suggesting a renal or renovascular source of bleeding.

[Clinical segment 2] A 55-year-old man with end-stage renal disease on thrice-weekly hemodialysis presented with sudden onset of cramping right flank pain radiating to the groin. He denied fever, nausea, vomiting, bowel changes, or prior similar pain, and had been anuric for two years. His medical history included diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and ESRD secondary to diabetic nephropathy and hypertensive nephrosclerosis; he had no history of trauma or prior renal procedures. On arrival, heart rate was 120 bpm, blood pressure 130/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. Examination revealed tenderness at the right renal angle; the remainder of the abdominal and systemic examination was unremarkable.

[Clinical segment 1] Her 54-year-old father reported over 10 years of progressive blurred central vision and color vision defects. He had myopia (–3.0 diopters) and no other relevant family history. Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/200 in both eyes. Intraocular pressures were 17 mmHg in the right eye and 16 mmHg in the left eye. Fundus examination revealed macular atrophy and lesions bilaterally. FAF imaging showed an outer ring of increased autofluorescence with central hypoautofluorescence in the macula of both eyes. OCT demonstrated loss of the ellipsoid zone and collapse of the outer nuclear layer in the central macula bilaterally. ff-ERG showed delayed implicit times in the dark-adapted 0.01 ERG, an electronegative waveform in the dark-adapted 3.0 ERG, and non-recordable photopic and 30-Hz flicker responses in both eyes.

[Clinical segment 1] A 48-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and hypertension presented with bilateral breast lumps of one-week duration. She had no family history of breast or ovarian cancer and had previously regular menstrual cycles. A core-needle biopsy of the left breast confirmed infiltrative duct cell carcinoma that was estrogen- and progesterone-receptor positive. On the basis of the physical examination results, the right breast lump was suspected to be a fibroadenoma. Hence, lumpectomy was performed.
